thread.title: BlackBerry: Did Investors Sour On The $1.4 Billion Cylance Deal? - BlackBerry Ltd. (NYSE:BB)

author: Shock Exchange
title: BlackBerry: Did Investors Sour On The $1.4 Billion Cylance Deal? - BlackBerry Ltd. (NYSE:BB)
text:
Cylance CEO Stuart McClure. Source: Forbes
Last week BlackBerry ( BB ) officially announced its $1.4 billion acquisition of Cylance, a leader in artificial intelligence ("AI") and cybersecurity:
BlackBerry Limited (NYSE: BB; TSX: BB) today announced it has entered into a definitive agreement to wholly acquire Cylance , an artificial intelligence and cybersecurity leader, for US $1.4 billion in cash, plus the assumption of unvested employee incentive awards ...
“Cylance’s leadership in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity will immediately complement our entire portfolio, UEM and QNX in particular. We are very excited to onboard their team and leverage our newly combined expertise,” said John Chen, Executive Chairman and CEO of BlackBerry. “We believe adding Cylance’s capabilities to our trusted advantages in privacy, secure mobility, and embedded systems will make BlackBerry Spark indispensable to realizing the Enterprise of Things.”
BlackBerry CEO John Chen does not appear prone to hyperbole; he used the word "indispensable" when describing the potential for BlackBerry and Cylance to exploit the Enterprise of Things ("EoT"). If the deal is so strategic then why is the stock down over 8% since news of the deal was leaked on November 9th. The market's reaction appears that investors soured on the deal.
Cylance Fortifies BlackBerry's Leading EoT Secure Communication Platform EoT enables digital transformation using hyperconnnected things in a highly secure environment. BlackBerry has a leading position in the EoT space. Its QNX software is embedded in more than 120 million cars. The company expects QNX to become embedded in even more cars, trains, corporations, etc. Growing connected things means the need for cybersecurity to protect them. Security is considered one of the top technical barriers to EoT success.
Cylance's AI solution predicts and protects networks against known and unknown threats. Its system identifies threats and analyzes them several months before they appear. Its AI solution has been deployed for 3,500 active subscription customers in over 15 million endpoints. Cylance's technology is expected to complete BlackBerry Spark, an EoT platform for ultra-secure hyperconnectivity. BlackBerry Spark enables OEMs to make autonomous vehicles and industrial equipment with the highest levels of security and safety-certification.
Cylance is expected to provide coveted AI and next-generation endpoint cybersecurity capabilities. BlackBerry/Cylance could usher in a world where OEMs can manufacture complex things with the utmost security, and consumers can trust any hyperconnected thing.
Can Cylance Fend Off Competitors? Cylance wants to secure every endpoint in the world. Its AI technology processes massive amounts of data. Cylance's AI gets smarter with every piece of data it scans by learning which features are malicious and which are not. If an attack bypasses AI security, humans can parse through the data breach and update the machines to guard against similar threats.
With AI becoming such a sought-after technology a major question is, "Can Cylance fend off competitors?" On the BlackBerry conference call Cylance CEO Stuart McClure spoke to the AI competitive landscape and why Cylance should win long term:
Stuart McClure - You asked about a couple of folks. One that's one of a more traditional anti-virus company and one that would be ... more of a detect and respond technology ... Today's attacks and just the sheer volume of these attacks and complexity of attacks just can't keep up with a signature-based approach.
We've been built up from the ground up ... with machine learning, artificial intelligence to actually predict attacks. We do far better, orders of magnitude better... when predicting brand new, unknown and knowns. When it comes to those traditional anti-virus companies the difference is clear for customers ... not just efficacy, but in simplicity and performance ...
From a detect and respond perspective ... first of all, we can truly replace antivirus completely on the endpoint. Whereas pretty much all the solutions still rely on an existing incumbent AV to stay on the box ... Second is we are truly open ... we do not require customers to give us their requirement. They can build their own detection capabilities, their reaction capabilities, their response capabilities, and it makes a very flexible platform ...Lastly, we can truly prevent both online and offline, which is really key. Whereas, pretty much all of those other vendors can't.
Cylance's ability to replace antivirus complete at the endpoint, online and offline could make it a differentiator among other next generation competitors. I actually felt more comfortable with the company after listening to the conference call. I believe in McClure and Cylance's ability to execute.
Can BlackBerry Afford Cylance? I understand Cylance generated $130 million of revenue in its recent fiscal year. Revenue also grew 90% Y/Y. The deal is valued at 10x trailing revenue. Based on Cylance's growth trajectory it could be valued at 7x to 8x forward revenue. The 10x revenue multiple dwarfs BlackBerry's own valuation - BB trades at less than 4x run-rate revenue of $840 million (recent quarter's revenue annualized). BlackBerry had $2.2 billion of cash and securities prior to the acquisition. It will likely be under $1 billion when BlackBerry reports its next quarterly earnings.
BlackBerry's operating cash flow through the first six months of its fiscal year was $22 million. This was equivalent to a rounding error for much larger firms like Apple ( AAPL ) or Microsoft ( MSFT ). There is no evidence Cylance makes more or is cash flow positive. With Cylance's current growth trajectory, it could chew up a lot of working capital - a commodity BlackBerry now has less of.
BlackBerry could be cash flow challenged post-transaction. Based on Cylance's value-added to BlackBerry's security offerings the deal makes sense strategically. Financially it may not pay off for a while. This should be concerning to investors and could explain why BB sold off after news of the deal leaked.
Another point of contention could be the state of the U.S. economy. Selling security for connected cars, trains, et. al is key to BlackBerry's future. How many connected things will be sold if the economy falters? Industrial production grew 0.1% for the month of October, down from nearly 0.2% in September. This was dismal in my opinion, but consistent with the prevailing theme that U.S. economic expansion is getting long in the tooth.
As alarming is that motor vehicle assemblies appear to have peaked. The metric was 10.8 million in October 2018 - flat Y/Y - but well off the post-crisis peak of 12.6 million set in July 2015.
Source: St. Louis Fed
How many connected things will OEMs produce and sell, and how many will BlackBerry secure if the economy falters? How many connected cars will BlackBerry/Cylance protect if auto assemblies decline due to a sagging economy and weak consumer?
Conclusion For the Cylance deal to work financially BlackBerry needs the economy to hold up. I highly-doubt that it will. Sell BB.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
